segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m glad you came.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I am, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: From the beginning, I’m going to tell you why we’re doing this.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Hawa, OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At some time, the kids are going to start listening to what it’s like to talk good Cherokee. Someday your children might want to listen to you talking Cherokee, they will let them listen.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Hawa, OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The first thing—what is your English name?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Joyce Marie Green Shell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In Cherokee?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Ag ti uya s ga wo di.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What year?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: February 6th, 1951.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like there at Greasy, growing up?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: When I realized at that time—my grandpa—his name, Tsu Seabolt was my grandpa’s name; we lived with him when we were growing up. They were all Cherokee speakers, and that’s what they talked all the time. At that time our aunts—my Aunt Susan, my grandpa, and Knutsu—they all lived there. All of Susan’s and her kids lived there. We all lived there. At that time, we all just talked Cherokee. Grandpa and Knutsu both, and my uncle, always planted a big garden. They all helped the people living close to us with their gardens. They would also help each other plow. Grandpa was raising pigs, they would be all over the bluff. Back then the livestock were free to go anywhere. When he would feed them in the evening-time, they would all come up.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: The older brothers would help. It was like that when I was little. After that, when I was growing up and starting going to school, I remember they wouldn’t let me talk Cherokee in school. They told me I had to talk English. When I would get to school, they would tell me that. I remember my teacher. I was having a hard time talking and reading in English. When I got to the second grade they kept me back. They sent me back to the first grade, they told me I had to learn English. As I was growing up, Dad moved us to a different house down the hill. But we were all raised up in church at Greasy. That’s what we were taught. Our mom and dad—their names were Waleli and Neli. When we would get to church, they would say, “You kids are going to sing today.”

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: That’s when it all started, we’ve been singing since. I guess they taught us, but they told us to sing when we got to church.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you kids what did you all do? For instance, playing, what could you do back then?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I don’t remember having anything to play with. They would just make something. We would be in the woods or close to the water. We had a big area of water where my granny aunt and mom would wash the clothes. We would play around while they washed the clothes. Then growing up, they were making everything for us to play with. As for the boys— those Ones had things that were flat and about that long [gestures]; [tins] that used to have tobacco in them—they called them ‘Prince Albert’ back then. They were making cars out of them, back then; and the wheels were made out of wire. And [they would] push them around. Or, they would [roll] a tire around—old tires that they found, when we were growing, that’s what they would do. Us girls, they would make us dolls. We would play in the woods, at the creek, or underneath trees, and make a play area. There was something like a broom—it grew so tall. You can’t hardly find it anymore. Back then it was growing everywhere in the fields—we would break those and tie them together to make brooms. We would sweep and clean our play area. Everything that we had to play with was homemade, or they would teach us how to make it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many was in your family?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: When I was growing up, there was 12 of us. But there were two women that were my second cousins, and one man that was my second cousin.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All together how many?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I guess there was 14 of us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did all of you speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: All of us grew up speaking Cherokee. ’Till this day, when we get together, we still talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I finished eighth grade there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you finished there, where did you go?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: What they called UG. Now they call it Cave Springs, now. That’s where I went to school.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: When I finished there, I went to the big school in Tahlequah—what they call Northeastern. I just needed, like, a little more time to finish there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you mentioned that that One did gardening, what were they planting?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Ah, they were planting everything. I remember they had us pulling weeds. They would plant corn, potatoes, onion and lettuce, radish, and carrots. He also planted strawberries—two, three, or four rows.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How were they plowing it?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Grandpa had a one-wheel plow that he pushed. It plowed good by pushing it. He also had horses that he used. And we rode the horses, too. That wasn’t all they did. We were always riding horses. All of us-that-were-younger would ride five-at-a-time on a horse.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they canning?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: They were canning. When it was time to can, we had to help—dig potatoes, pick corn—we were helping with that, too. I remember my feet were dirty.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She still has dirty feet.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: From digging the potatoes. I remember, a long time ago, there were big grease-buckets with handles—that’s what we would put them in. They would tell us to, “Set them right here as you fill them up,” or, “Dump them here,” they would tell us. We would leave again and get more. But the older ones did more of the heavy stuff; but us smaller ones were just in the way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How were they putting up the potatoes?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I know when Dad was gardening, he would dig up a lot, then he would dig a hole and put them back in there, and cover it up. Or—what do you call those buildings these days? And they had a place to hang the meat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Smokehouse.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Smokehouse, smoker or smoked is where they hung the meat, they also put the potatoes in there and everything. Also when we picked the green beans my aunt and mom would can them and put them up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Grandpa had pigs.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Grandpa had pigs, I remember he would be saying, “Sooey, sooey!” They would all come out of the woods when he would call them. On this month when it’s cooling off, they would start killing the pigs—about three or five within one week.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: The neighbors would all help. They would make the oldest boys help.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you women do at that time?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: We would do the cleaning. Like the guts—they didn’t throw anything away back then, when they would kill something, they would fix it. At that time, us women or girls—when Mom and Aunt would boil them, after the boiling they would put them in another pot; after they cooled off—they would send us over to that, and they would tell us to, “Clean them like this.” Sometimes, after you cleaned them, we would turn them inside out. You had to pull them—they would give us little peach limbs we would hold that, and pull it, and twist it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were turning them inside out?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: We were turning them inside out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you ate the guts you’re talking about?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I’ve tried them, I never liked them. I still see them in a store, bagged up. You can see them. But I haven’t tried them. I know what they are, and where they came from. I don’t know if that’s why I don’t like them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That might be it.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I guess it stinks.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yes, it stinks, I don’t know if they stink as much—what they have in the store.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I know you couldn’t do it. What did you think when they weren’t allowing you to talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: It was a little strange to me, because that’s all I knew. I used to think, “What’m I going to say now?” But when I would tell Dad they wouldn’t let me talk Cherokee, he would get mad and go to the school. He would tell them, “You’re not going to stop my kids from talking Cherokee, because that’s all they know.” He was saying that for a few years. He would get mad when we would tell him that happened during school. Then he started to understand that we had to learn those things. “To grow up and learn,” he said, “You’re going to have to learn—the White man has to teach you to learn the English language. You will have to depend on that, growing up.” When he told us that he was against them telling us that. When he told us, “You have to learn now,” it was a little hard. I realized it was hard for me to speak it (English). These students that are going to school here, I notice they have a hard time talking Cherokee or learning it. I think that what was happening to me when I was trying to talk English and learn. That’s what was happening to me. The Cherokee is having a hard time learning Cherokee. I think that’s what was happening to me. I try a little harder from them to hear me when I’m talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many kids do you have?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Four girls, and I’m raising my grandchild.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: They understand it, but they don’t talk. They can say a few words, but they can’t converse all Cherokee with me. But I talk to them in Cherokee, and they understand me. They will answer me back in English when I talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about Dad, your dad, what did he do to support the family?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: When summer would come, he always leaves to go to Colorado. He cut broom; he also worked on the railroad when we were little. I remember sometimes it would just be Mom and all of us. Grandpa and my aunt, and all their kids. We all lived at Grandpa’s.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you do now?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Right now, I’ve been here for six months at the school. The Cherokee school is where I’m working. I teach Cherokee, I’m a speaker.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you do in the past?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I worked where they built houses—the Housing Authority. Also, I started at Cherokee Nation as a Cherokee speaker, translating and filling out paperwork; for helping Cherokees if they needed help, if Cherokee Nation could do it.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I helped with filling out the paperwork. Also, they put me where all the Cherokees were just English speakers. I would go over there and fill out papers for what they needed. Then I would bring them back to Cherokee Nation. So, they could get help for their needs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did you work there?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: All together for three years, then I stopped. Then I went to where the White people worked, for three years; it was called Eastern Oklahoma Development Center. They also helped the elderly.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I worked with the older worker program. So, it’s been since 1997 when I started working with Cherokee Nation. I quit for three years and came back. I’ve been here for 27 years at the Housing Authority, where they build houses. I came from there, and now I’m here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s go back, what kind of cooking stove were they using at that time?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Wood, wood stove. They had two stoves. If we’re talking about when I was growing up, they had two stoves. They had one cook stove in a room, and one cook stove outside. They would cook beans all day long. In the evening when it was time to cook supper, they would finish cooking inside, in the room. There was always food, and leftover food. We had leftovers of everything. They put up bread from the morning. When we would go outside, that would give us that for a snack. We were always outside. They had a snack—when we would get hungry, we would all eat bread. If there wasn’t enough bread while we were playing, we would all cut it for us all to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: About that, tell us about when you first learned how to make bread.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Ha, when Mom died, I was eight years old. She was sick, but as I was growing up, she made me learn how to cook. There were all boys living, and the older women... my brothers, I mean my sisters, they had already left, got married and had kids. Then me, Dad, Waleli, and Neli were left. There were only three of us there, [and] there were still three of the oldest boys staying there—they weren’t married yet. At that time, I had to learn to make bread. “Get a chair,” she would bring me a chair. I would stand on a chair making bread my dad would say, “You have to do it like this.” He would put flour in a big deep bowl and set it out. He would put flour in it. He would set it out for me. My dad would set me out warm water, at that time he would warm it up. We didn’t have running water. We lived inside the house. That’s when I started making bread. When they were cooked, they would be dry and hard just that big [gestures]. So, then I would set them out to feed the boys.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We were looking for a hammer.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: They didn’t like them [loaves], but if you see them around, they turned out good—because they’re old now. They’re still alive, even though they had to eat hard bread. Even though they didn’t like them—but they’re still alive.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Even gravy isn’t that easy when you try it, at first. That’s what I tell the boys. They’re always saying, “I would like to eat mom’s cooking.” I tell them, “All you need to do is learn to fry bread, or make gravy.” They would say, “Boy, I can’t do it.” “You have to keep trying it’s going to get better.” I tried for a long time to make it like my mom’s [gravy]. I don’t know how many times I tried, but I can get it close—really brown. At first, it was turning out white, I guess I wasn’t letting it cook enough.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: You weren’t waiting for it to get brown. You were putting water in it too soon.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Because you were hungry, you were in a hurry.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Because I was in a hurry.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Were you making water gravy?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Water, water.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Sometime I use milk, and I also use water.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Sometimes milk. To me it’s easier to use the leftover grease after you fry meat.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yes, that’s good to use.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: When you went to Cave Springs, they called UG —somebody else said that yesterday.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I heard that before.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What is that?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Union Grade.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh that’s it?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I think that’s what they called it, at that time.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Union Grade, huh? When did they change that?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I don’t know when they changed it. When I started high school in ninth grade, they were calling it Cave Springs.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Who was talking about that, they were calling it UG?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It was ah, Ross.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Oh, it was Velma Gonzales.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, she was talking about that.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I think she went to school there, too. If you went to Greasy, you would go there for the higher grades.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And the closest.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yes, the closest.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The other was Stilwell, they didn’t really like the Indians. For instance, when I was going to school, we had good ballplayers. Two of them went to Stilwell, and they wouldn’t let them play.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Even if you were a good player, they don’t appreciate it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Cave Springs was a little like that, too. Especially Rocky Mountain and the kids that went to Cave Springs, it was mostly them. Not unless you were a really good ballplayer.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: They would appreciate you.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you started at Greasy, who was the principal at that time?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Nellie Mays.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Me too, how long do you think she was in there?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, I don’t know.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: She was probably the only principal as long as that school was open.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: As a girl I went to school there, it was Nellie Mays. When I finished eighth grade, it was still Nellie Mays.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The same for me. And the same for Udell, for a long time.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: DJ, too.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: For me, my teacher’s name was Sally Spares. She sent me back to the first grade. I had to start from there again.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you remember Wayne Isaacs?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I remember Wayne Isaacs, but he taught my kids.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: He came later.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yes, he came later.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I guess he had one short leg—because he had one thick heel on his shoe. About this [gestures] wasn’t it? He was a funny man.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He would come over and buy pigs from me. He would say, “Well how much you going to take me for?” He would say, “Boy you’re killing me.” Did you all have electric, back then?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: We didn’t have electric —just kerosene lighting is what they used. When they would go to another room, they would take it. If you were setting in that room, and they left, you would just be sitting in the dark. Then here, we would all be going—

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: —following the light

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: —following the one carrying the light.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Just a little after dark you all must have went to bed.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: There was nothing to do.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: No. In the summertime when they would get hot. We would lay the homemade mattress on the porch—made from plucked chickens and made into a mattress. They didn’t waste anything. When they would pluck the chicken, they would put them in a bag. When they would dry up good, they would put them in something to make a bed.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Make a mattress.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Uh-huh, make a mattress.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And pillows, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: And pillows, uh-huh. Also, when they would buy flour, at that time there would be good decorations, such as flowers and such. They would put them all up, and wash them. They would wash and dry them to make pillowcases. Or, I would be wearing a dress, or if somebody needed a dress, she would make her one [from the material]. They made their own things, and they sewed theirselves, and made quilts. I don’t remember... If somebody’s clothes got too little, or if somebody didn’t want their shirt or pants, they would make a quilt with it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How often did you all go to town?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Monthly, sometimes longer. If someone’s shoes tore up, and they had to get another pair, they would just take that One. That One would get new shoes. Then, the next month, if somebody else needed shoes. They would get new ones—they would take that One. We all had the same shoes—black with white stripes is what would be wearing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The rest of us—boots.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: The boys wore what they call ‘work boots’, nowadays. The boys would wear the same thing.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Talking about the black and white shoes, were they called Oxfords?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Oxfords.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Those were good ones.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: It was Oxford in English. I remember when they would bring me to Stilwell Mercantile [Store], they would take me to them. I would have the same shoes on, but new ones. It was funny.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mom put stuff up and canned. Did you learn the same thing?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I learned the same thing. These days I can my own. When you could find cucumbers, I canned my own cucumbers. Little Wa le li’s wife will give me some stuff. If they give him too much, then I can it. He gave me the cucumbers that I canned.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I was growing stuff.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Beets, too. They were giving me beets, and I canned those. Also jelly and stuff. Sweets and everything, I can. Tomatoes, I canned tomatoes, too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How would you say ‘beets’ in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Aww, I forgot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don’t remember.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Ga tlv s g is what I know.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Gi ge.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: A gi ge ga tlv sg—gige gatlvsg, I would understand it if somebody said that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Gi ge.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: If somebody told me, “Do you want to can gige gatlvsg?” I would understand it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: If they said that, I would probably understand it. Sometimes, the Cherokee, you just can’t say what it is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You have to talk about it.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: You have to talk about it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: In English, you have to describe it.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: That’s how it is to talk Cherokee—it’s all visual. Just by seeing it, you’re going to talk about it. That’s what I tell them when I’m teaching. “When you talk Cherokee it’s visual, you describe, you talk about it. What it is, what color, and how big it is. If it’s wood or cloth.” You would say, “I’m wearing a red blouse.” For men it’s tsu nv wu and for women tsu na ti tle d. That’s what I tell them there’s a difference.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I heard a man saying a wa ti l di.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: “You don’t have a blouse. You have my shirt. You have your shirt on.” If it’s a woman, “I have my blouse on.”

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: A lot of them say that, don’t they?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, the men.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I had a white blouse, tsa wa ti l dv, on. What about the blouse, di tli d. When they were playing, they would say we won blouse, di thl d.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Really? That’s interesting—Wa le le, “You don’t have a blouse on.” Don’t be saying that. “You have a red shirt on.” Also, men would say, “I have a short sleeve on, I’m wearing a short sleeve. I’m wearing different colors, striped or different colors.” And women would be, “Blouse.” But nowadays if women are talking about what they’re wearing they would say, “A wa nv wv,” they wouldn’t say, “A wa thl dv.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This morning my sugar got low. I thought I was going to church. I thought it was Sunday. I had my Sunday shirt on. My wife asked me what I was doing. I told her I was getting ready. She said, “Are those your Sunday clothes?” I told her, “Well it’s Sunday.” She pulled this out and I put it on. I was told that, “We need to leave as soon as possible.”

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Ha. Me, yesterday—everybody has a phone; they think it’s important. Everybody has a phone. I got an email to wear a flannel shirt tomorrow, and boots. ‘Flannel shirt and boots day tomorrow’ is what the email said. That’s why I’m wearing these. Sometimes our class does that. They say, “Let’s wear this, it’s somebody’s birthday. And let’s bring something.” Since I’m a part of that, and I want the kids to know I’m doing right by them. A little like we’re all together, when we’re doing the same thing. All of us in that, in this room, are a group; and plus, the ones in the second room are a group. We all should be nice, love and help one another, and get along. How would you say it—they call it ‘ cohesive’ if the whole group did the same thing. We can be one, so everybody knows we belong. We’re all involved. And we all are a group, and that makes us one. They understand that. That’s why I think sometimes they’re watching me—but I’m glad they understand what I’m telling them. But, sometimes you have to talk to them a little, and then they will understand it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long would you say that we sung? How many years?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Just what I could sing, when they asked me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m talking about our group.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Oh jeez, a long time ago, a long time. How old were you?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I wasn’t 20 yet.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Maybe, a long time ago.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Probably 30 years ago.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Or longer, longer... at that time it was just our family singing, then. At that time, your nephews started singing. Playing guitars and beating drums is what they did. I’m going to tell my age, it was a long time ago. About, Lord 40, 30 [years ago].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s about that. I know it’s 30, though. Maybe more.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yeah, 30... 30 or 40 years since we’ve been singing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you all were living with your grandpa. I don’t know if I was born then.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: You were alive, but you were a baby.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you all got sick, did they take you to the doctor?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: No we didn’t go to the doctor. Either our grandpa, aunt, mom, or dad doctored us. There was an old lady name Sa da ni. Sa da ni’s house was about a mile away. She doctored us. When I realized it was her doctoring me for anything, even if I had a earache.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was she doing, when she was doctoring your ear?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: She would use warm water, or coals, and blow toward my ear. And some kind of grease—I didn’t know what it was, I never knew what it was. I didn’t ask. I just thought they were doctoring me and I was going to get well. My parents were depending on that—to get doctored. I don’t know what kind of grease it was. She would put it in a small spoon and heat it up. Then she would pour it in my ear. She didn’t use what they call a ‘dropper’ these days, that you pour with. She wasn’t using anything like that. I don’t remember seeing anything like that. But when the spoon would cool down, she would pour it in. She would put a little bit of cotton in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Cotton.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I guess ‘v wa n’ is cotton, right? I guess you would call it that, she would put cotton in there to close it off. When it healed, she would check to see if it was good.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Have you ever heard using a rattlesnake skin for earaches? Have you ever heard that?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Rattlesnake?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Vg shu di, rattlesnake.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are ‘vg shu di’ and ‘v tsu na di n’ the same?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ugh, that smell.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: So that’s ‘v tso na di’ right?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s when it’s a ‘tso tv s go’, when you smell that.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I thought the smell was kind of like a cucumber. Is what I thought, “The smell is like a cucumber.”

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That snake, ‘v tso na di’.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: What I noticed, it smells like a cucumber.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: And they say ‘tsa wa’, snake, smells the same. I’ve never smelled that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me either.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The black snake, too. It throws out a smell, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes the diamond back.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That’s why I was asking you if they were the same thing—‘vg shu di’ and ‘v tso na di’ were the same thing, [both rattlesnakes]?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Some of the diamond backs they call ‘v tso n’. Like the others, it won’t do it right off, until you make it mad.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: If it realizes you’re close, you can smell it. I wonder, “Why do I smell cucumbers and I don’t see a cucumber?” I think about that, so I watch where I go.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That’s what I heard—that ‘tsa wa’ rattlesnake smells like a cucumber. I’ve never smelled it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I’ve never smelled it either.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I should’ve paid attention, to see if it’s true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Right now they’re blind, they can bite you pretty quick.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They are scared. They’re looking for a place to go right now. I don’t know how to say the word ‘hobby’ [in Cherokee], do you have one?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Hobby? I would say ‘anything that you like to do’. Is what I would say ‘hobby’ is. I like to can. When all the kids in the family go to sleep, that’s what I do. That’s when, “I want this,” “Can you make this?” and, “Can you give me something to drink?” stops. When they go to bed, I’m by myself. I clean the kitchen really good. I wash their dirty dishes first. When I’m finished with all of that, I start canning. Because you have to clean the canning jars first, and the lids—you have to clean them good, they have to be clean. You’re going to can for nothing if they’re not clean—it’s going to ruin. Then you have to start over. That’s why I wait. After they all go to sleep at night, when I’m by myself, I can. If one of them smells what I’m cooking, they show up and ask me what I’m cooking. Then they wait for me to cook it and eat it. So, that happens.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Also when she said ‘gv ga’ that is specifically referring to a Mason jar, right?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yes—jar. Canning jar, to can with.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You would say ‘u lv sa da’ if it was a glass.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: If it was to drink with, uh, you would say ‘u lv sa da’, glass.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: ‘U lv sa da’, glass.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: You would say ‘u lv sa da’, glass.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like the-one-that-bites-you.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah, tick. That one.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: True.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: A lot of things are the same.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Another thing is, when you wake up in the morning, the sun comes in through the window—that’s de l v sa tv s gi, the sun rays. That also means ‘du lv sa dv ne’—like your, when you see the sun coming through, with a line that goes to the bottom, that word is ‘glass’, too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is the word ‘shadow’ the same—’i ga du lv sa du’—is it the same?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: You can call it that. If I’m talking about a shadow, it is like that—but if the sun is coming through. But you can tell if someone goes by, you can see a little light—it’s a shadow, it makes a shadow.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What us Cherokee believe in, like ‘tsk li’. Have you ever seen anything interesting?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: A little bit, not a lot. Just what Dad and Grandpa talked about, ‘tsk li’ is all I’ve heard. I remember when they would start talking about things like that, we would set good. After a while we would all be sitting close together. We would get scared while we were gathered around. As for myself, I don’t remember seeing anything like that before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then, there was a lot of visiting. For instance, when Grandpa would talk, did they let you kids listen to them talking?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: No, they didn’t let us listen to adults sitting around talking and having conversations. They would run us out. They would tell us to, “Go play outside.” At that time, she was fixing us lunch, and telling us to go outside. But they would set water out for us in a metal bucket with a dipper in it. That’s where we would drink water, when we were outside. Being outside. They didn’t let us stay in the room where adults were talking. They would tell us we’re “Not to listen to us adults talking,” they would say. “You all are just kids.” They would run us outside. A lot of times I would be at the window, wanting something. They would say, “Go play,” and send me away. It wasn’t just Mom or Dad. It was my aunts, Grandpa, and uncles—any adult would say that to you. They didn’t pick a specific person to scold you—when your parents were getting on to us. Anybody could scold you when you were doing something wrong. They would say, “Don’t do that, stop doing that, you’re not supposed to be doing that.” Anybody could say that to you. If we were at church, anybody could get on to you, or switch on the leg, scolding you when you were doing something outside. If you didn’t want to go to church, they would say, “You’re going in,” and they would get a switch. At that time, it was like anybody could scold you—when we were little. Even, the adults would have meetings at church—we weren’t allowed to listen to that neither. They would run us outside. At home where we lived, they didn’t let us listen while adults were talking. They would tell us to, “Go outside, play, and get out.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me ask you this—you all were always telling people I was mean. Was I that mean?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Yes, you were a crybaby, a tattletail—you couldn’t do anything without that he had to tell on you. Then they would switch our legs. And him, too. They would include him. When they whipped one—they whipped all of us. It wasn’t just one. We would be mad at the one that started it. We would be telling them that it was their fault that we got a whipping. Wa le li was mean—he would be in a tree, or I would be in a tree, when he’s hitting me with rocks, throwing the rocks. Until he would get caught. Then he would get jerked [away]. I’m surprised he has arms, because he was jerked around, because he was so mean.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they ever, I was probably too little... Did Dad and Grandpa ever mention about the Trail of Tears? Did they ever talk about if they were in that?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Not that I remember. The older brothers and sisters would know more of them talking about that. I don’t hear it, I was too little.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: A long time ago, when the elderly sometimes would say, “It’s going to be like this someday.” Do you remember anybody saying that? Do you remember somebody saying something like that, and it happened? I can give you an example—my uncle was telling me they were drinking water from a spring. They didn’t have running water in the house. He told me, “One of these days you will be buying water.” I thought that was crazy, why would I be buying water, it’s everywhere? Now I’m buying water.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: That’s what’s happening, that’s really what happens. When I was growing up, there were springs and that’s where we were drawing our water. When they would buy their milk... for instance there was a White man name Evert Denny who sold milk, he had cows. They would buy their milk there, and put in the spring to keep it cold. It would be in there. And butter from commodities. Still ’till this day, how they’re helping people get food, at that time when they were giving it to us. When we got the butter, they put it in a metal bucket. A lard bucket with a lid, and put it in there at that time’. I remember when we were living with Grandpa, they did that. There was a big spring—no water coming in the house. I remember they used to say that. That’s happening now. Sometimes I have a bill of 78 dollars, sometimes, for using water. So, I’m buying water, that’s what I’m doing. Another thing—groceries are so expensive. We going to be hungry, if you pay attention to the Bible that’s what it says. And it’s happening. It’s all coming true.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Boy what would we do if they closed Walmart? If something happened and they closed Walmart? What about the food? I don’t know if I can kill a deer, Charlie. Just that quick, I wouldn’t be able to find one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I would die pretty quick here on earth, if I had to depend on a deer.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I don’t even know if there’s anything living out in the woods. We’ve been talking about that. I guess there are some out there, if you can find it.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I haven’t seen any ka ni g’. Do you remember ‘ka ni g’?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Is that elderberry?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh. It was black, hanging like this [gestures]. It was black, you could eat it. It was to eat.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: And te la ni, too. You don’t see that anymore. I ate that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I’ll tell you why that’s not around anymore. It’s what Soldier said, right? He and Lilly were in here. Lilly said we were like cows when we were kids. She said, “We would tilt our heads up eating, ‘ka ni g’.” “There’s not any left,” she said, “You can’t find it anywhere.” Soldier said, “You all ate it up.” That’s probably why it’s gone, right?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: You can’t even find the trees these days, I realized, but I don’t think about it. When White people buy land, they put up a fence immediately. You can tell the land doesn’t belong to a Cherokee. They put up a fence as soon as they can. A Cherokee can’t get in even if you have a card showing you’re a Cherokee, that allows you to come in, they still won’t let you. They won’t even let you pick onions. I know one lady that had already picked it, and was carrying the onions. The wealthy owner saw her and asked her what she was carrying. She told him, “Onion.” He took it away from her.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Huh, it’s really like that. You can’t go anywhere these days.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Uh-uh. A while back I seen... what do you call those trees next to the road? Ha, I forgot how to say ‘persimmon’.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sal.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Sal—I thought it was something else. I was remembering it, but I wasn’t sure. I seen a persimmon tree on the side of the road. It didn’t look like the persimmon were ripe yet. I thought, “I’m going to remember. When they ripen, I’m going to get them.” That’s what I can’t understand why they’re so stingy with them. It’s just on this side of the fence, or under the fence. But I might get shot at. Some of them will do that to you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I was telling you all that, I found those grapes. If they would’ve found out. They could’ve put me in jail. That’s against the law. Arkansas is strict—they will really do that to you. One time we were coming back from Lincoln. Boy it was just covered with red. What do they call them ‘sand plums’? My wife said, “Let’s pick them.” So, I stopped and parked and quickly got out with a sack. I was really picking them up, thinking, “We’re gonna gather a lot.” After a while I looked around, she sitting in the truck. My helper. I told her, “You told me let get them?” They really will get you if they see you. We’re going to finish up now. What do you think is going to happen to our language?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I have a belief that, what I’m teaching—they’re going to learn it right. Not because I’m teaching it. They have to want to learn the language we give them. To continue to do good—to teach good, and to teach the ones coming in after them. This is what I tell them. I wish I could put all the words I know in a box. “Just by doing that, you all could learn.” I told them, “I would do that if I could do it. Then you all would know all of the words I gave you, use them, and teach with, and talk it.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you think it’s going to be like the way we’re talking now?

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: I don’t think so. I realize now, that it’s changing. If I say “Ko hi tsi g,” in full Cherokee and say, “Ko hi tsi gi” they’re going to say, “Ko hi.” They’re changing it, and making it shorter to speak in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s the way we talk.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: That is the way we talk. But if you give them the full word, are they going to understand, or know what that means? Nowadays when they write it down, they’re just reading what they’re writing. Do they understand what they’re reading?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This is what I hear from the students, “That’s different.” They will say, “Yo na.” When we talk, we would say, “Yo n.” When they make all those sounds, it is hard to understand what they’re saying. All of yo na tsi stu i, all of those sounds—to me is hard to understand, to me. But ‘yo na’, bear, ‘tsi s d’, rabbit, is easy to understand, to me.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: But you have to give them the whole word.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess they tell you that.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That word ‘yo n’—if you write that in syllabary it’s ‘yo na’.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It says ‘yo na’.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: The fluent Cherokee speakers knows you can cut it off, to make it shorter.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Cut the tail off the word.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: They need to learn. They want to put the English words into Cherokee. It doesn’t seem like that to me. Sometimes we don’t have another word to describe it. That’s all we can do is to say the same thing—in Cherokee, then English—and it won’t work. Sometimes it can happen. Sometimes, someone in North Carolina will ask how to say something. I read it, and it doesn’t say that in Cherokee. I read, and it doesn’t say that in Cherokee. It’s a White man’s thinking, “I can probably do that. But I can put in a long but descriptive.” That’s what a Cherokee says, a real Cherokee. They want it to be exactly parallel.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: That won’t work.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It can’t happen.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Cherokee is backwards. That’s what I realized here—when they write long sentences. If I say it in Cherokee, I have to say it backwards. They’re putting it all like you would in English.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Just like speaking English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m glad you came. We’re finished.

segments.speaker: joyce-green
segments.translation: Me too.
